entries.text: My night patrol runs the same eleven checkpoints in the same order, and after twelve years my boots know the route better than my eyes do.
I was at checkpoint seven when the breach alarm sounded, two decks and four minutes from Sector C at a dead run.
When I reached the corridor the pressure doors had already sealed, and through the port glass I could see that there was nothing left for anyone to do.
Lena Voss once stayed up two full shifts helping me rebuild the duty roster after the flu wave, and she never mentioned it to anyone.
I altered one line of my patrol log last month to hide the twenty minutes I spent letting a contraband medical shipment through the cargo airlock.
The contraband crates were insulin and fever strips for the lower deck clinic, bought off-manifest because requisitions kept stalling, and I let them through twice.
If the investigation pulls my raw patrol telemetry, the altered line will not match the door sensors, and no one will believe it was only medicine.
In twelve years my section has never lost a person to violence, and I have signed every incident report myself, even the embarrassing ones.
Three days before the breach I watched Ilya Soren stand outside the records office for ten minutes doing nothing, and I decided not to log it, and I keep returning to that decision.
I felt something was wrong in Sector C that week, a maintenance pattern that didn't fit, and I filed nothing because a feeling is not evidence.
I start every shift with black tea in a dented thermal cup and a walk past the brig, which has been empty for two hundred days and I intend to keep it that way.
Young officers think security is about catching people; it is mostly about being seen in the right corridor at the right hour so nothing needs catching.
Lena told me her audit would ruffle Operations more than Security, and asked me to keep a corridor quiet for her walk-throughs, which I did.
The lower decks queue for the clinic before first shift, and the line has gotten longer every quarter for two years; I count it every morning without meaning to.
From the security ring the sunrise hits the solar arrays edge-on, and for about a minute the whole truss looks like it is burning without heat.
I keep thinking that if I had logged Ilya outside the records office, Lena might have walked a different corridor, and I carry that arithmetic everywhere now.
My mother was a customs officer on the old orbital, and she used to say the uniform is a promise you make to strangers.
I secured the corridor perimeter for six hours after the breach, logging everyone who approached, including two engineers I sent away twice.
The man who moves the medical shipments knows my name and my shift pattern, and that knowledge is a hook in my mouth I put there myself.
Patrol logs are signed, timestamped, and mirrored to the central grid; I teach every recruit that a log you would not swear to is a confession you haven't finished writing.
Ilya Soren has pulled my people out of two bad pressure drills, and half of Security owes him a drink they have never paid.
I sleep four hours in the first rest cycle and two in the second, a habit from convoy duty that peace has never managed to break.
Sitting across from the detective I keep a running list of which questions could touch the altered log line, and so far none of them have.
We call flare season winter up here, and during it my radios crackle like old campfire recordings from a world I have only seen in archives.
The canteen holds my table by the door without being asked; a security chief who sits with her back to a room teaches the room the wrong lesson.
The last time I spoke to Lena she asked whether I trusted the maintenance logs, and I said I trusted the people who wrote them, and she said that wasn't what she asked.
The clinic nurse who takes the off-manifest insulin never asks where it comes from, and I have decided that if this ever surfaces, her name stays out of it no matter what it costs me.
I run breach drills on fourth-days and time every section with a stopwatch older than most of my officers; Sector C always posted the best seal times on the station.
I handed the investigation my full patrol route, my door badge history, and my radio transcript within an hour of being asked, before counsel could tell me not to.
Some nights I rehearse the sentence that would end my career — I changed one line in one log — and it is somehow heavier than the whole breach.
